corpus_definition: worth a lot of money or very important

forms.definition: how much money something is worth, or how important or useful it is
forms.example: The value of this old house has doubled in ten years.

syn.note: Very close; worth is a little less common as a noun.
Easy word. The price is what you pay in a shop; the real value can be higher or lower.
Used for the 'very important' meaning: the importance of education.

forms.definition: an expert's opinion of how much money something is worth
forms.example: The bank asked for a valuation of the flat before giving the loan.

forms.definition: to think that someone or something is very important; also, to decide how much money something is worth
forms.example: I really value my friends from university.

syn.note: Close; appreciate also means 'be thankful for'.
Stronger and warmer: you treasure memories or gifts from people you love.
A little formal; often used in the passive: 'highly prized'.
You respect a person's ideas or work; value is wider.

forms.definition: worth a lot of money, or very useful and important
forms.example: Keep your valuable things in the hotel safe.

syn.note: Very close for jewellery, metals and things you love: precious stones, precious time.
Easy word; expensive is only about a high price.
Easy word for the 'very important' meaning: useful advice, valuable advice.
Stronger: so valuable that you cannot put a price on it.
Easy word; used when something is not about money.

ant.note: Having no value or use at all.
Easy word: costing little money.
Not useful in any way; opposite of the 'very important' meaning.

forms.definition: extremely useful or important, so useful that nobody can say how much it is worth
forms.example: Your help with my English homework was invaluable.
forms.note: False friend: in- here does NOT mean 'not'. Invaluable means even more useful than valuable. The opposite is worthless.

forms.definition: thought to be very important and useful by other people
forms.example: Dilnoza is a valued member of our team.

forms.note: There is no common adverb; valuably is very rare.

people.definition: small things you own that are worth a lot of money, like jewellery
people.example: Please do not leave your valuables in the car.

context.text: My grandmother's old carpet from Bukhara is very valuable. An expert came to do a valuation, but we will never sell it. We value it because she made it by hand.

reviewer_note: Trap: invaluable is a false friend (in- does not mean 'not'); kept as an existing extra with a note and no in- affix. Valuables (plural noun) placed in People & things.

corpus_definition: Extremely large in size, area, or amount.

forms.definition: the very great size of a place or area
forms.example: We were amazed by the vastness of the desert.

syn.note: Very close but more formal and less common.
Easy word; size can be big or small.
A wide open area of land, sea or sky.

forms.note: There is no verb made from vast.

forms.definition: extremely large in size, area or amount
forms.example: Uzbekistan has vast deserts in the west.

syn.note: Easy and very common; almost the same meaning.
Almost the same meaning.
Almost the same, a little more formal.
Easy word, but much weaker than vast.
Covering a large area or including a lot: extensive gardens.

ant.note: Easy word: extremely small.
Easy word: not large.

forms.definition: very much; to a very great degree
forms.example: Life in the city is vastly different from life in the village.
forms.note: Used before adjectives and verbs: vastly different, vastly improved.

syn.note: Very close; a little informal.
Close; often used with verbs: greatly improved.
Easy word: much better, much bigger.

ant.note: A little; to a small degree.

context.text: The Kyzylkum is a vast desert. When you stand in it, you feel small next to its vastness. Travel there today is vastly easier than it was a hundred years ago.

reviewer_note: vastly means 'to a great degree', not 'in a vast way'; definition written for that use.

corpus_definition: A tube that carries blood back to the central organ.

forms.definition: one of the thin tubes that carry blood back to your heart
forms.example: The nurse found a vein in his arm.

syn.note: Any tube that carries blood; veins are one kind.
An artery carries blood away from the heart; a vein carries it back.
A very thin blood tube between arteries and veins.

forms.note: The verb vein (to mark with thin lines) is very rare and not used by learners.

forms.definition: having thin lines that you can see, like blood tubes under the skin
forms.example: My grandfather's old hands were thin and veined.
forms.note: Also used for leaves and stone: veined marble.
There is no adverb made from vein.

context.text: When I gave blood in Tashkent, the nurse looked for a vein in my arm. My grandmother laughed and showed us her veined hands. She said her veins are easy to find.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same body meaning merged into one map; the medical adjective venous is from Latin, not made from vein, so it is left out.

corpus_definition: a risky new business activity or project

forms.definition: a new business or project that might fail or lose money
forms.example: They launched a new business venture together last year.

syn.note: Close; also means a company or business in general.
A big job or project; formal and less about risk.
Easy word; a project is not always risky or about business.
Easy word: a company that sells things or services.

forms.definition: to start doing something new and risky, especially in business
forms.example: Last year the company ventured into the Russian market.
forms.note: Usually 'venture into' or 'venture out'. It can also mean to go somewhere that might be dangerous.

syn.note: To do something that could have a bad result.
To be brave enough to do something.
In business: to grow into new places or markets.

forms.note: Venturesome is rare. Adventurous is made from adventure, a different word today, so it is not shown here.
There is no adverb made from venture.

context.text: My cousin in Samarkand started a small venture selling dried fruit online. It went well, so last year she ventured into the Kazakh market too.

reviewer_note: Venture capitalist and joint venture are compounds and left out. Adventure/adventurous treated as not_family (separate words today).

corpus_definition: A doctor who treats sick or hurt animals.

forms.definition: a doctor who treats animals that are sick or hurt
forms.example: The veterinarian helped my cat feel better.
forms.note: Mainly American English. British English says vet or veterinary surgeon.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.

forms.definition: to check a person or a document carefully before accepting them
forms.example: All new teachers are vetted before they start work.
forms.note: Belongs to vet = check carefully, not to an animal doctor's work.

forms.definition: connected with the medical care of animals
forms.example: She studies at a veterinary college in Samarkand.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from veterinarian.

people.definition: the short, everyday word for an animal doctor
people.example: We took our dog to the vet on Saturday.
people.note: Much more common than the long word in British English.

context.text: Our dog was sick, so we took him to the vet near Chorsu Bazaar. The veterinarian said he only needed rest. She works in a big veterinary clinic.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); vet goes in People & things. Verb vet (check carefully) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: By going through or using a certain route.
usage_note: via + place: travel through a place on the way (fly to London via Istanbul). via + method: using something to send or get it (send it via email).

relations.note: Easy word; 'through' is very common for places on a journey.
Same meaning for routes, a little more formal.
Formal; used for the method, not the route.
Easy word for the method meaning: send it using email.
Going straight from one place to another, without stopping: a direct flight.

context.text: We flew from Tashkent to London via Istanbul. The ticket was cheaper than a direct flight. I sent the photos to my family via Telegram.

reviewer_note: Kind corrected to function (preposition). Both uses (route and method) covered in the usage note.

corpus_definition: A person who watches a television program.

forms.definition: a person who watches a TV programme or a video
forms.example: The show attracted millions of viewers worldwide.
forms.note: programme (British) = program (American).

syn.note: Easy word, but much less common.
The whole group of people who watch; one viewer is one person in the audience.
A person who watches a sports event live, not on TV.
A person who watches something happen in the street.

forms.definition: the activity of watching TV, films or videos
forms.example: This film is not suitable for family viewing.

forms.definition: what you can see from a place, or your opinion about something
forms.example: Our flat has a beautiful view of the mountains.
forms.note: Belongs to view = what you see or what you think, not to watching TV.

forms.definition: to watch a TV programme, film or video
forms.example: The video was viewed two million times in one week.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with the same meaning.
Easy word: 'Did you see the match?'
To turn your eyes to something, often for a short time.

forms.note: There is no common adjective; viewable is rare.
There is no adverb made from viewer.

context.text: Millions of viewers in Uzbekistan watched the football match last night. Many young people viewed it online, not on TV. Evening viewing is very popular in our family.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6). Noun view (scene/opinion) is other_meaning; viewpoint is a compound and left out.

corpus_definition: Physical force used to hurt or kill people.

forms.definition: using physical force to hurt or kill people
forms.example: The movie contained too much violence.

syn.note: Angry behaviour that may become a fight; it is not always physical.
Very cruel physical force.
Easy word: people hitting each other or a war.
Physical strength used to make something happen; not always to hurt.
Making people or animals suffer; it can be without physical force.

ant.note: Easy word: a calm time with no fighting.
Not using force, even to protest. Also spelled non-violence.

forms.note: There is no verb made from violence. Violate (to break a law or rule) looks similar but comes from a different word.

forms.definition: using physical force to hurt people, or likely to do this
forms.example: The police arrested a violent man at the market.
forms.note: Also used for very strong weather or feelings: a violent storm.

syn.note: Angry and ready to fight; not always physical.
Very cruel and violent.
Easy word: not gentle, using too much force.
Angry and frightening, often used for animals and fights.

ant.note: Calm, with no fighting.
Easy word: kind and soft, not using force.
Not using force to protest or get something. Also spelled non-violent.

forms.definition: with a lot of physical force, in a way that can hurt people
forms.example: The two men argued violently outside the cafe.

syn.note: In an angry way, ready to fight.
In a very cruel way.
Easy word: without care, using too much force.

ant.note: Calmly, without fighting.
Easy word: softly and carefully.

context.text: There is no violence at our school in Fergana. If a student becomes violent, the teachers call his parents at once. Last year two boys argued violently, but a teacher stopped them.

reviewer_note: violate is not_family (different Latin root). Negative forms nonviolence/nonviolent placed in ant lists, not as forms.

corpus_definition: Very important or necessary for life.

forms.definition: a lot of energy and enthusiasm
forms.example: My grandfather is eighty, but he is still full of vitality.
forms.note: Belongs to vital = full of energy and life, not 'very important'.

forms.definition: to give new life and energy to a place or an activity
forms.example: The city plans to revitalize the old part of Bukhara.
forms.note: Belongs to vital = full of energy and life, not 'very important'. British spelling: revitalise.

forms.definition: extremely important or necessary, especially to stay alive
forms.example: Water is vital for all living things.

syn.note: Almost the same: completely necessary.
Almost the same: extremely important for what happens next.
Easy word, but a little weaker than vital.
Easy word, but much weaker than vital.
Very important, often in a serious or dangerous situation.

ant.note: Not important at all.
Not needed.
Small and not very important.

forms.definition: in an extremely important or necessary way
forms.example: It is vitally important to drink water in the summer heat.
forms.note: Almost always used in 'vitally important'.

syn.note: In a way that is extremely important.
Easy word: very, very.
Completely: absolutely necessary.

context.text: Clean water is vital for the farms in Khorezm. In summer, it is vitally important not to waste it.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: vitality and revitalize belong to vital = full of energy, so they are other_meaning. Vitamin looks related but is a separate word; left out.

corpus_definition: Doing a task for no pay to help others.

forms.definition: doing work to help other people without being paid
forms.example: He likes volunteering at the local animal shelter.

syn.note: Work for a charity, often unpaid; very close.
Easy phrase; it does not always mean helping others.
Work that helps the local area; sometimes a court orders it as a punishment.

ant.note: Work that you are paid for.

forms.definition: to offer to do a job or help without being paid
forms.example: My sister volunteers at a children's hospital every Saturday.

syn.note: Easy word: to say you will do something.
Easy phrasal verb: to help, often for a short time.

ant.note: To say no when someone asks you to do something.

forms.definition: done because you want to, often without being paid
forms.example: She does voluntary work at the library on Sundays.
forms.note: voluntary work = volunteering.

syn.note: Easy word: you get no money for it.
You can choose to do it or not.
Easy word: costing no money; free work = unpaid work.

ant.note: Something you must do because a rule says so.
Easy word: you get money for it.

forms.definition: because you choose to, not because someone makes you
forms.example: Many students voluntarily stayed after school to clean the park.

syn.note: Happily and because you want to.
Without anyone forcing you.

ant.note: When you do not want to do it.

people.definition: a person who offers to work without being paid
people.example: The volunteers cleaned the park in one day.

context.text: My sister enjoys volunteering at a children's hospital in Tashkent. She volunteers every Saturday. All the work there is voluntary, so nobody gets paid.

reviewer_note: volunteer is both the verb (forms) and the person noun (People & things); volunteer noun placed in people per rule 8, not repeated in the noun slot.
